error.signature: AI tells someone that every home or apartment in Switzerland already has, or is guaranteed, its own ready-to-use nuclear/civil-defense shelter nearby

verdict.summary: Switzerland's Bevölkerungs- und Zivilschutzgesetz (BZG, SR 520.1) Art. 46 does set a national policy of one protected place per resident, and about 370,000 private and public shelters exist. But the obligation to build a private shelter (Schutzraumbaupflicht) has applied only to new residential buildings of 38+ units since a 2012 reform; smaller developments and most existing older or newer small buildings have no shelter of their own, and the owner may instead pay a CHF 1,400-per-place replacement levy (Ersatzabgabe, BZG Art. 46/47) that funds public shelters elsewhere. BABS itself documents 'cantonal differences and local gaps,' especially in city centers and growing areas. Assigned personal shelter spots are also not pre-communicated in peacetime - allocation happens only if the security situation requires it.

dead_ends.action: Assume any specific apartment building or house in Switzerland has its own private nuclear/civil-defense shelter simply because Swiss law guarantees 'one shelter place per resident' nationally
dead_ends.why_fails: Since the Federal Council's 2012 revision, the private shelter-building obligation (Schutzraumbaupflicht) under BZG Art. 46 applies only when constructing residential buildings with at least 38 apartments; smaller buildings are routinely exempted on payment of a CHF 1,400-per-place replacement levy (Ersatzabgabe) that funds public shelters instead, so a typical single-family home or small apartment block built after 2012 has no on-site shelter at all, and older small buildings are not retrofitted.
dead_ends.condition: Buildings with fewer than 38 residential units, especially built or renovated after 2012
dead_ends.common_misconception: That the famous 'every Swiss person has a guaranteed bunker spot' fact means every individual building has its own physical shelter on site.

dead_ends.action: Tell someone they already know, or can find out in advance, exactly which shelter they are assigned to in peacetime, the way a fire-evacuation plan works
dead_ends.why_fails: BABS states shelter places are allocated ('zugewiesen') only if the security-policy situation requires it - there is no standing peacetime personal assignment communicated to residents by default, so someone expecting a pre-known personal shelter number will not find one until authorities actually activate the allocation process during a crisis.
dead_ends.condition: Peacetime, no active civil-protection emergency declared

workarounds.action: Ask the building administration/owner (Verwaltung) or the communal civil protection office (Zivilschutzstelle) whether the specific building has a registered private shelter, and where the nearest public shelter is, rather than assuming coverage
workarounds.how: Cantonal civil protection offices maintain shelter registers; residents can also consult cantonal pages (e.g. Kanton Zug, Aargau, Thurgau civil-protection shelter pages) that list public shelter locations by municipality.
workarounds.condition: Wants to know actual, current shelter coverage for a specific address

frequently_confused_with.distinction: That canon covers which number to call for an active emergency; this one covers whether a physical civil-defense shelter is actually available near a given home, which is a separate, commonly overstated claim.
